name: Marketing Coordinator - Well Aligned Poor Performance - Loomly
description: Marketing Coordinator at Loomly, an early-stage e-commerce brand. Both employee and manager agree the employee has underperformed during a rough quarter — missed campaign deadlines, sloppy work quality, and communication gaps. Rare aligned-poor scenario: both parties tell a consistent story about the underperformance and the reasons behind it (personal stress plus role that was over-scoped for a coordinator level). Tests whether the brief handles genuine agreement on weak performance cleanly and produces low but well-supported scores without triggering the misalignment classifier.

answers.employee: I'm a Marketing Coordinator at Loomly. I've been in the role for about eight months. My core responsibilities are running the weekly email campaigns, coordinating with the design team on creative assets, updating the product pages when there's a launch, and pulling basic performance reports for my manager. Realistically the scope this quarter was heavier than a coordinator role usually carries — with the Series A push, I was also asked to help draft landing pages and coordinate with an outside PR agency, which is closer to a marketing manager's job. I want to be upfront that I don't think I handled the expanded scope well. The stretch was real and I underperformed on it.
answers.manager: The employee is a Marketing Coordinator at Loomly, in role about eight months. The core scope is exactly what she described — weekly email campaigns, creative coordination with design, product-page updates, and basic performance reporting. That is the coordinator scope she was hired for and it's what she should be evaluated against. What is fair context, and I want to name it clearly, is that this quarter we asked her to stretch into landing-page drafts and PR-agency coordination because of the Series A push. That work is above the coordinator level. I own the decision to hand it to her, and it was too much. So the evaluation should hold her to the coordinator scope, with the acknowledgment that even inside that scope this quarter did not go well.

answers.employee: The goals that mattered were: send twelve weekly email campaigns on schedule, hit the target open rates, coordinate the creative for the Q3 product launch, and support the Series A landing pages. The email schedule was clear. The Series A work was less clear — I never had a concrete brief, deadlines shifted, and honestly by the time I understood what was being asked, the deadlines were already close. I did not communicate that clearly enough at the time. That's on me.
answers.manager: Her recap of the goals is accurate. The weekly emails and the Q3 launch coordination were well-defined at the start of the quarter. The Series A scope was rolled out on the fly as the fundraise moved and I did not brief it well — that is a real gap on my side and I want to say so on record. Success measures were: send twelve weekly campaigns with two or fewer misses, hit a 22 percent open rate average, ship the Q3 launch creative on time, and support the landing-page cadence. She and I both understand those were the numbers.

answers.employee: The results were below what I wanted. On the email campaigns, I sent nine out of twelve on schedule — three were late and one didn't go out at all because I missed the segmenting step. Open rate averaged around eighteen percent against a twenty-two percent target. The Q3 launch creative went out but the launch email itself had a broken discount code that I did not catch, and we had to send a follow-up apology to customers. On the Series A landing pages, I helped, but the outside agency ended up rewriting most of what I drafted. Honestly, my impact this quarter was neutral to negative and I know that.
answers.manager: Her account matches the numbers. Twelve weekly campaigns targeted, nine sent on schedule, one never sent — that is a real business miss. Open rate averaged eighteen percent versus the twenty-two percent target, meaningfully below plan. The broken discount code on the launch email caused about a hundred customer complaints and a same-day apology email that I approved. On the Series A landing pages, the outside agency did rewrite most of the draft work she produced. The one bright spot was the Q3 launch coordination itself with the design team, which she owned and executed cleanly — that piece went well. So the picture is: one clean win, several concrete misses, and a stretch project that did not land.

answers.employee: Execution was my weakest area this quarter. The three late email sends were mine, and the reason was I did not build enough buffer into my week and small blockers cascaded. On the discount-code error, I did not run a final QA pass before sending — I was tired and I skipped a step I know is required. I own that. On the Series A work, I should have raised the flag much sooner that I was underwater instead of trying to power through. When I did finally say something, it was two weeks later than it should have been. I do not think my reliability this quarter reflects my usual standard, but I understand it is what happened and I am not going to argue with the record.
answers.manager: Her honesty about the causes is accurate. Three late sends and one missed send is a reliability problem that I have to reflect in the review. The discount-code error is on her — the QA checklist exists specifically to prevent that, and it was skipped. On the Series A escalation, I agree with her: it came two weeks late and I would have restructured her workload if she had told me sooner. That said, I want to note something honestly: I saw the workload building and I did not check in on it either. So the late escalation is on her side of the ledger, but the reason we got there is on both of us.

answers.employee: Quality slipped. The discount-code error is the clearest example. Beyond that, two of the email campaigns had typos that customers replied about. I know the standard for the role and I did not meet it this quarter. When I look back at what caused it, I was distracted — I had some difficult things happening outside of work that I let bleed into how I was operating — and I stopped running my usual checklists. That is not who I want to be at work and it is not who I am when things are normal.
answers.manager: Work quality was clearly below her usual standard, and I want to be honest that her usual standard is genuinely good. This quarter had the discount-code error, two typo campaigns that got customer replies, and one product-page update where the pricing was wrong for about six hours before someone else caught it. I have known her long enough to know this is not her baseline. She has told me she was dealing with things outside of work — I believe her — and I think that is part of the honest story of what happened this quarter without excusing the outcomes.

answers.employee: Communication was mixed. Day-to-day with the design team was fine — they will tell you we worked well together. The gap was upward. I did not tell my manager I was overloaded until it was too late. I did not flag the discount code issue until customers were already complaining. Basically, when things got hard I went quieter instead of louder, which is exactly the opposite of what I should have done.
answers.manager: Day-to-day collaboration with design was strong — that team specifically told me she is easy to work with. The gap was in escalation to me, and she has described it accurately. When workload got heavy or when something went wrong, she went quiet and tried to fix it alone. That is the pattern I most want to work on with her next quarter. It is not a professionalism problem — she is professional and respectful in every conversation — it is a communication-under-pressure pattern that I think we can coach.

answers.employee: On judgment, the specific calls I got wrong were: not asking for help on the Series A work sooner, and not running the QA checklist before the launch send. Both were preventable. On growth, I have learned more about the business this quarter than in the previous six months combined — the Series A stretch, even though I did not do it well, taught me a lot about how marketing scales. I am not ready for a marketing manager role and I do not think I should be evaluated as if I were. I want to get back to running the coordinator role at a high standard first. That is what I am ready for.
answers.manager: I agree with her on all of it, honestly. The two specific judgment calls she named were the exact two I would have named — the late escalation and the skipped QA. Both are addressable. On growth, she is right that she is not ready to move up yet, and I want to be clear that the answer for next period is not promotion, it is recovery — getting the coordinator role back to a high standard, rebuilding reliability on the emails, and practicing early escalation. If that goes well over one or two quarters, the growth conversation opens up again.

answers.employee: The context that matters is: I had things going on outside of work that affected me, my scope this quarter was above coordinator level, and I did not raise my hand when I should have. None of those excuse the misses. But I do think a fair evaluation names them alongside the misses. For next quarter what I need is a scope that is squarely coordinator-level, a weekly check-in with my manager where I have to say if I am underwater, and permission to use the QA checklist even when a launch is running late. Those are three things that would help me get back to my normal standard.
answers.manager: The context she named is fair and I agree with all of it. On my side, I want to name that pushing coordinator-level scope into landing pages and PR-agency coordination was a mistake that I own, and it made a hard quarter harder. For next period my expectations are: coordinator scope only, twelve weekly campaigns with zero missed sends and no more than two late sends, QA checklist non-negotiable on every send regardless of timing, a standing weekly one-on-one with an explicit workload check, and one clear escalation channel for when she needs help. If those are in place, this becomes a very recoverable situation and I fully expect her to recover from it.
